tasks.short: Learn about market conditions, technical developments and regulations through publications, sales meetings and trade events.

steps.what: Find relevant publications, event agendas and industry updates.
Read publications and record relevant market, technical and regulatory developments.

loop.input: Retrieved publications, source dates and territory priorities.
loop.output: Market notes with linked passages, dates and uncertain claims.
loop.check: Check source links and dates automatically; representative checks material claims against original passages.
loop.stop: One extraction and one repair per document; unreadable or unsupported material goes to the representative.
loop.why_not_simpler: Free text expresses developments in varied language; keyword alerts cannot reliably explain their relevance.

steps.what: Attend trade sessions and discuss developments with customers, suppliers and peers.
Judge commercial implications and identify questions requiring technical or regulatory verification.
Share the reviewed brief with relevant sales and technical colleagues.

tasks.design: Configure source subscriptions and reading queues in the {EMAIL} and {DOCS}; use a bounded extraction loop to prepare linked market notes. A {WORKFLOW} distributes the representative's reviewed brief and feeds a territory view in the {BI}, while trade conversations and commercial interpretation remain human.
tasks.previous_blocker: Publications use inconsistent language, and event knowledge often stays in personal notes. Source alerts alone do little interpretation.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing subscriptions handle collection. Bounded text extraction can prepare cited notes, while AI-assisted coding reduces the effort of connecting sources and territory records.
tasks.still_hard: Source licensing, incomplete coverage and checking regulatory meaning remain costly. Informal conversations contain context that publications miss.
tasks.human_edge: The representative tests credibility through relationships and distinguishes a technical novelty from a buying trigger.

ambition.what: Weekly territory-level review of emerging demand signals

tasks.altitude: The week contains less source searching and more focused conversations. The representative can propose territory experiments sooner; pricing and product investment rights do not change.

reach.task: Recommend a territory experiment from emerging demand signals.
reach.learn: Segment sizing, evidence thresholds and experiment evaluation.

evidence.claim: Source alerts, dashboards and bounded summaries with links can support market monitoring.
The digest provides no documented case establishing savings for trade-event learning.

assumptions: This baseline represents a mid-size European technical-products seller.
Meetings remain the largest time component, consistent with the supplied priors.
Build ranges estimate working effort for a narrow pilot, not elapsed approval time.
Public sources dominate; account-linked notes require GDPR controls. Applicable EU AI Act duties and national rules need assessment.
unknowns: Which publications permit automated retrieval and summarisation?
Which source subscriptions and territory records are accessible?
How much attendance serves learning versus relationship development?
Would the proposed reporting introduce employee monitoring requiring consultation under national rules?
research_questions: Which sources repeatedly change account conversations or territory choices?
Can reviewers trace each material claim to a current primary source?
new_work: Review extracted claims and uncertain regulatory statements.
Maintain source permissions, subscriptions and territory filters.
Remove duplicate stories and stale alerts.
Track whether demand signals lead to useful experiments.

tasks.short: Sell service contracts that match customers' technical products, operating needs and commercial constraints.

steps.what: Check installed products, current coverage and service history.
Discuss downtime, operating requirements, budget and service expectations with the customer.
Select an eligible service package and calculate its price.
Prepare the service offer using approved scope and contract wording.
Review scope, price and terms before sending the offer.
Negotiate service commitments and resolve the customer's objections.
Sign the agreed service contract.
Record the signed coverage and hand over activation details.

tasks.design: Connect the {CRM}, {ERP}, {HELPDESK} and {CLM} to assemble coverage and configure eligible service packages using explicit rules. Generate offers from approved templates, gate their release in the {WORKFLOW}, and use the {ESIGN} completion event to record coverage and request activation. Needs discovery and negotiation stay with the representative; nonstandard commitments follow the existing approval policy.
tasks.previous_blocker: Installed-base records, service history, prices and contract terms sit in separate systems. Package eligibility and exceptions are often poorly documented.
tasks.enabler_now: Existing configuration and signature features cover much of the process. AI-assisted coding makes the missing data links and document generation cheaper to build; no model loop is necessary.
tasks.still_hard: Legacy equipment, ambiguous coverage and unusual response commitments need technical and commercial judgement. Integration cannot repair an inaccurate installed base by itself.
tasks.human_edge: The representative uncovers the customer's real downtime exposure and negotiates credible commitments with service operations.

ambition.what: Offer standard service coverage to smaller installed-base accounts

tasks.altitude: The representative spends less time assembling offers and can reserve conversations for service risk and objections. Standard offers stay within existing delegated limits; concession authority does not expand.

reach.task: Assess whether an installed product qualifies for a service package.
reach.learn: Equipment compatibility, exclusions and the evidence needed for technical escalation.

reach.task: Recommend which uncovered account segment should receive a service campaign.
reach.learn: Coverage penetration, service capacity and contribution margin.

evidence.claim: Elfsquad provides configuration and quoting linked to ERP and CRM; this supports the configuration pattern, not every service-contract rule.
The ZARGES vendor case reports quote preparation falling from about 15 minutes to 90 seconds; applicability to service contracts is unproven.
Approved templates and signature-triggered record updates can automate standard contract paperwork.

assumptions: Standard service packages have codifiable eligibility, pricing and approved wording.
The baseline includes customer signature time; it is not all representative labour.
Material changes after negotiation return through offer review and any required concession approval.
Build ranges estimate working effort for one product family; formal consultation may add elapsed time.
GDPR controls apply to contact and service data; employee monitoring requires assessment under national rules.
unknowns: Are installed products and existing coverage reliably linked to customers?
Which configuration and document features are already licensed?
Who may approve discounts, exclusions and service-level exceptions?
Can service operations honour each package in each territory?
What access approvals or employee consultation are required?
research_questions: Which eligibility rules cause most manual checks?
Does lower preparation cost make smaller-account coverage commercially viable?
new_work: Maintain package eligibility, price versions and approved clauses.
Resolve unmatched installed products and coverage conflicts.
Review released offers and route concessions to authorised approvers.
Monitor failed activation handoffs and duplicate coverage records.

tasks.short: Demonstrate technical or scientific products safely and explain how they fit the customer's intended use.

steps.what: Arrange participants, location, equipment availability and demonstration time.
Assemble approved instructions and examples for the customer's application.
Inspect equipment, prepare the setting and check safe operating conditions.
Demonstrate operation and adapt the explanation to participants' understanding.
Answer application questions and identify limits requiring specialist follow-up.
Record findings and assign technical follow-up.

tasks.design: Configure booking in the {CALENDAR} and {WORKFLOW}, then generate a versioned demo pack from approved material in the {DOCS} and application fields in the {CRM}. A short structured form records findings once and creates follow-up in the {PROJECT}; the representative reviews the pack, checks physical conditions and conducts the demonstration.
tasks.previous_blocker: Application examples and manuals are scattered, while booking and follow-up require repeated entry. The central demonstration depends on physical conditions and participant reactions.
tasks.enabler_now: Template assembly, scheduling and linked forms are ordinary deterministic capabilities. AI-assisted coding reduces the effort of connecting them without generating new operating instructions.
tasks.still_hard: Safe operation, unusual applications and judging participant understanding remain human work. Approved content must match the actual equipment version.
tasks.human_edge: The representative notices unsafe handling, hesitation and misunderstanding, then changes the demonstration immediately.
tasks.altitude: Preparation and follow-up shrink, leaving more attention for application fit and participant understanding. Demonstration responsibility and decision rights stay unchanged.

reach.task: Define acceptance criteria for an application demonstration.
reach.learn: Test design, measurable performance limits and escalation criteria.

reach.task: Develop a reusable explanation for a common operating problem.
reach.learn: Instructional sequencing and checking participant understanding.

evidence.claim: Scheduling, approved-template assembly and structured follow-up can reduce demonstration administration without automating physical delivery.
The digest supplies no documented case of automating a physical technical-product demonstration.

assumptions: This baseline is an in-person demonstration requiring physical equipment.
Booking automation uses customer-requested times and available equipment within defined scheduling rules.
Approved templates contain selectable examples; no model creates operating or safety instructions.
Build ranges estimate working effort for a narrow pilot.
GDPR applies to participant records; recording or employee analytics would need a separate assessment under national rules.
unknowns: Which products require specialist certification or additional safety checks?
Are current manuals and equipment versions reliably linked?
How often are demonstrations remote rather than physical?
Which application fields can be captured without burdensome forms?
What access or employee consultation is needed for the proposed workflow?
research_questions: Which preparation items repeat enough to become approved templates?
Can the booking workflow reliably reserve both equipment and qualified staff?
new_work: Maintain approved examples and manual-version mappings.
Review generated demo packs for application fit.
Resolve booking conflicts and missing equipment records.
Check that technical follow-up reaches the responsible specialist.

tasks.short: Translate customer application needs into useful feedback for product design teams.

steps.what: Gather customer comments, application details and supporting account evidence.
Clarify the customer's underlying problem, constraints and business impact.
Write a technical feedback brief with examples and commercial context.

loop.input: Validated customer need and permission-filtered account evidence.
loop.output: Structured feedback brief separating observed facts, requested features and unverified interpretations.
loop.check: Require evidence links; check required fields automatically; representative verifies technical meaning and customer attribution.
loop.stop: One draft and one correction pass per brief; missing evidence stays explicit and routes to the representative.
loop.why_not_simpler: Customer language varies, and producing a concise problem statement requires contextual interpretation.

steps.what: Discuss application trade-offs and possible adaptations with the product design team.
Decide whether to investigate, defer or reject the requested adaptation.
Record the disposition, responsible owner and next review date.
Explain the disposition and agreed next step to the customer.

tasks.design: Link account evidence from the {CRM}, {EMAIL} and {HELPDESK} to a structured feedback record in the {PROJECT}. A bounded drafting loop prepares an evidence-linked brief for representative review; deterministic rules synchronise the design lead's disposition and generate a customer status draft. Technical trade-offs and product commitments remain human decisions.
tasks.previous_blocker: Feedback is spread across account notes, messages and service records. Product teams receive feature requests with inconsistent evidence and little account context.
tasks.enabler_now: Linked records and structured intake already solve routing and follow-up. A small text loop can turn varied customer language into a reviewable brief without choosing the product roadmap.
tasks.still_hard: Customer requests may misidentify the underlying problem. Commercial importance, engineering feasibility and competing customer needs require discussion.
tasks.human_edge: The representative tests what the customer actually needs and translates between commercial urgency and technical constraints.

ambition.what: Weekly cross-account prioritisation of recurring application gaps

tasks.altitude: The representative spends less time assembling evidence and chasing dispositions. They can bring a stronger cross-account recommendation to product discussions; engineering priorities and delivery commitments remain with the product design lead.

reach.task: Turn an application complaint into a testable technical problem.
reach.learn: Operating envelopes, acceptance criteria and separating symptoms from causes.

reach.task: Compare commercial impact across accounts requesting similar adaptations.
reach.learn: Pipeline weighting, segment bias and evidence quality.

evidence.claim: Structured intake, linked account evidence and bounded drafting can reduce feedback preparation and follow-up work.
The digest contains no documented case proving automated product-design feedback or prioritisation.

assumptions: The baseline includes product design lead time and therefore is not entirely representative labour.
Explicit account and product identifiers support collection; semantic similarity never silently merges customer needs.
The design lead records a structured disposition, allowing automatic downstream synchronisation.
Build ranges estimate working effort for a narrow pilot; formal consultation may add elapsed time.
GDPR, confidentiality controls and applicable EU AI Act duties apply; employee monitoring requires assessment under national rules.
unknowns: Which customer evidence may be shared with the product design team?
Are account, product and service records consistently linked?
Who may make product commitments or communicate expected dates?
How does the product team currently prioritise requests?
What access approvals and employee consultation are required?
research_questions: Do structured briefs improve disposition speed or reduce repeated clarification?
How can cross-account views avoid over-weighting large or vocal customers?
Which feedback fields predict a useful engineering investigation?
new_work: Review drafted briefs for technical fidelity and supported claims.
Resolve missing account links and duplicate feedback records.
Maintain intake fields, access controls and status templates.
Check that customer updates avoid unapproved delivery promises.
Review recurring application gaps across accounts.

role.altitude: The representative's week shifts from collecting records and preparing documents toward application discovery, demonstrations and credible service conversations. They gain capacity to recommend territory experiments and cross-account priorities, while commercial exceptions and product commitments retain their existing approval rights.
reach: Sales engineer: frame testable application needs and recognise technical escalation points.
Sales manager: recommend segment experiments and service-coverage priorities.
Demonstrator and product promoter: develop reusable explanations and check customer understanding.
skills_to_grow: Translate technical customer language into measurable requirements.
Validate source-backed summaries and distinguish facts from interpretations.
Understand service eligibility, exclusions and contribution margin.
Use structured evidence to compare needs across accounts.
Design safe demonstrations with clear acceptance criteria.
role.ambitious_version: A technically credible account adviser who connects market signals, installed-base service needs and application evidence, then proposes focused commercial experiments and product investigations.

job.title: Sales Representatives, Wholesale and Manufacturing, Technical and Scientific Products
